# Overview of eating disorders

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Obstetrics/gynecology > Menstrual cycle and associated disorders > Overview of eating disorders*

[Original Article Link](/library/GP0BTT)

---

## Summary

Eating disorders are complex, multifactorial conditions characterized by disordered eating and/or weight control behaviors. They are associated with serious negative physical and psychological outcomes, including mortality. Conditions include <u>anorexia nervosa</u>, <u>bulimia nervosa</u>, <u>binge eating disorder</u>, <u>pica</u>, <u>avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder</u>, and <u>rumination disorder</u>. Although any individual can develop an eating disorder, <u>adolescents</u>, athletes, and individuals with comorbid psychiatric conditions and/or a history of trauma are most commonly affected, and these individuals may benefit from routine screening. Individuals with a suspected eating disorder require a comprehensive clinical and laboratory evaluation. The diagnosis is confirmed if the relevant <u>DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for eating disorders</u> are fulfilled. Most patients can be successfully managed in an outpatient setting, however, intermediate care settings such as <u>partial hospitalization programs</u> and residential care may be more appropriate for some patients. Those with <u>red flag features of eating disorders</u> require inpatient medical or psychiatric hospitalization. Management should involve a multidisciplinary team and consists of <u>nutrition support</u> and education, including weight restoration if necessary; <u>psychotherapy</u> (e.g., <u>family-based therapy</u> for <u>adolescents</u>, <u>cognitive behavioral therapy</u> for adults); and, for some patients, pharmacotherapy (e.g., <u>SSRIs</u> for <u>bulimia nervosa</u>, <u>lisdexamfetamine</u> for <u>binge eating disorder</u>). Although complete recovery is possible, a chronic, relapsing course with progressive deterioration is common.




<u>Anorexia nervosa</u>, <u>bulimia nervosa</u>, <u>binge eating disorder</u>, and <u>pica</u> are further detailed separately.

## Overview

See the respective articles for details.




### <u>Binge eating disorder</u> [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)[[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)[[4]](/library/cm1aeh0)




Most common eating disorder in adults in the US




* Key features

* Recurrent <u>binge eating episodes</u> that are not associated with <u>inappropriate weight compensatory behaviors</u>

* Pronounced <u>obesity</u> at a young age is common; <u>BMI</u> may also be normal.

* See also “<u>DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for binge eating disorder</u>.”

* Management

* <u>Psychotherapy</u> (<u>CBT</u>, <u>interpersonal therapy</u>)

* Pharmacotherapy may be considered in select patients.

* Management of comorbidities (e.g., <u>ASCVD prevention</u>)





> [!TIP]
> Weight compensatory behaviors are seen in <u>anorexia nervosa</u> and <u>bulimia nervosa</u> but not in <u>binge eating disorder</u>. [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)

### Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder (<u>ARFID</u>) [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)




#### Key features (all must be present)




* Avoidance or restriction of food

* ≥ 1 of the following:

* <u>Significant weight loss</u>; slow growth trajectory (in children)

* <u>Malnutrition</u>

* Dependence on <u>nutrition support</u>

* Impaired psychosocial function

* Features are not explained by <u>body image disturbance</u>, cultural practice, <u>food insecurity</u>, or another medical (e.g., gastrointestinal disease) or psychiatric (e.g., <u>anorexia nervosa</u>) condition.





#### Management




* See “<u>Initial evaluation of individuals with a suspected eating disorder</u>.”

* Nutritional <u>rehabilitation</u>: similar principles as those used for <u>weight restoration in individuals with anorexia nervosa</u>. [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)

* <u>Prevent refeeding syndrome</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Complications of <u>ARFID</u> can be similar to the <u>associated features of severe malnutrition in anorexia nervosa</u>. [[13]](/library/y_1dIj0)




### Rumination disorder [[5]](/library/b01He20)[[14]](/library/dZ1o020)




* A syndrome characterized by recurrent <u>postprandial</u> food <u>regurgitation</u>, without preceding retching  [[14]](/library/dZ1o020)

* Considered both a functional gastrointestinal disorder and an eating disorder





### <u>Pica</u> [[15]](/library/yn1dDh0)[[16]](/library/xn1Evh0)




#### Key features




* Persistent ingestion of nonnutritive nonfood substances

* Complications (e.g., dental damage, GI symptoms) may be present depending on the substance consumed.

* See also “<u>DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for pica</u>.”





#### Management




* Identify and treat underlying etiology (e.g., <u>iron deficiency</u>, <u>electrolyte</u> abnormalities) and complications (e.g., <u>malnutrition</u>, <u>lead poisoning</u>).

* Behavioral interventions

* Consider <u>SSRIs</u> for refractory symptoms.

---

## Clinical features

* Clinical history [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)

* Body image disturbance: distorted perception of one's body and associated dissatisfaction with one's appearance

* Fear of weight gain

* Changes in eating and/or exercise patterns

* Social stressors related to appearance or weight

* Weight fluctuation (e.g., weight loss, inadequate weight gain for height, rapid weight gain)   [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)

* Signs of <u>malnutrition</u> [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)[[5]](/library/b01He20)[[17]](/library/bm1HVh0)

* Neurological: <u>seizures</u>, <u>weakness</u>, <u>dizziness</u>, <u>headaches</u>

* Cardiovascular: <u>palpitations</u>, <u>cardiac arrhythmias</u>, <u>orthostatic hypotension</u>

* Metabolic: <u>secondary osteoporosis</u>, <u>stress fractures</u>, <u>euthyroid sick syndrome</u>, <u>hypothermia</u>

* <u>Secondary amenorrhea</u>, <u>oligomenorrhea</u>, <u>delayed puberty</u>

* <u>Lanugo</u>

* <u>Hair</u> loss; <u>brittle nails</u> and <u>hair</u>

* Muscle wasting

* <u>Edema</u>

* Fatigue

* Poor <u>wound healing</u>

* Signs of recurrent <u>vomiting</u>  [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)[[5]](/library/b01He20)[[17]](/library/bm1HVh0)

* <u>Caries</u> and <u>perimolysis</u>

* <u>Russell sign</u>

* <u>Sialadenosis</u>

* Oropharyngeal <u>petechiae</u>

* Gastrointestinal symptoms [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)[[5]](/library/b01He20)[[17]](/library/bm1HVh0)

* Abdominal discomfort and/or <u>bloating</u>

* <u>Nausea</u>

* <u>Vomiting</u>; possible <u>hematemesis</u>

* <u>Constipation</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Relative energy deficiency in sport</u> is not itself an eating disorder, but can occur concurrently with or lead to the development of an eating disorder. Ensure all athletes are <u>screened for eating disorders</u>. [[18]](/library/f61k430)

---

## Initial evaluation

### Approach [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)[[5]](/library/b01He20)




* Perform a clinical evaluation in patients with any of the following:

* Positive <u>screening for an eating disorder</u>

* Suggestive clinical features, e.g.:

* Rapid change in weight

* Significant deviation from growth trajectory on <u>CDC longitudinal growth chart</u>

* Delay in <u>pubertal development</u>

* <u>Oligomenorrhea</u> or <u>amenorrhea</u>

* Confirm the diagnosis.

* Make a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> based on the <u>DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for eating disorders</u>.

* Consider the following based on clinical suspicion:

* Exclude organic causes of weight changes and eating behaviors.

* Evaluate for alternative or comorbid psychiatric condition (e.g., <u>depression</u>, <u>OCD</u>).

* Further evaluation

* Evaluate for <u>complications of eating disorders</u>.

* Screen for <u>red flag features of eating disorders</u>; determine disposition.

* Initiate management specific to the disorder.

* If <u>BMI</u> ≥ 25 kg/m<sup>2</sup>, perform a comprehensive assessment of patients who are <u>overweight or obese</u>.

---

## Diagnostics

### DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for eating disorders [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)




* <u>DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for anorexia nervosa</u>

* <u>DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for bulimia nervosa</u>

* <u>DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for binge eating disorder</u>

* <u>DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for pica</u>





### Evaluation for complications




#### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)[[5]](/library/b01He20)[[17]](/library/bm1HVh0)




##### Routine studies




* <u>CBC</u>

* <u>CMP</u>

* <u>Phosphorus</u>

* <u>Magnesium</u>





##### Additional studies




* <u>Malnutrition</u> and/or <u>significant weight loss</u>

* <u>Prealbumin</u>

* <u>TFTs</u>

* <u>Lipid panel</u>

* <u>Vitamin D</u>, <u>vitamin B12</u>, <u>iron</u>, <u>thiamine</u>

* Self-induced <u>vomiting</u>: alpha-<u>amylase</u>

* <u>Dehydration</u>: <u>urinalysis</u> (for <u>urine specific gravity</u>) [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[5]](/library/b01He20)

* <u>Pancreatitis</u>: <u>lipase</u>

* <u>Oligomenorrhea</u>, <u>amenorrhea</u>, <u>delayed puberty</u>, and/or long-standing eating disorder [[5]](/library/b01He20)[[21]](/library/s_ctpU0)

* All patients: <u>FSH</u>, <u>LH</u>, <u>TSH</u>

* Women: urine <u>pregnancy test</u>, <u>estradiol</u>, <u>prolactin</u>

* Men: <u>testosterone</u>





> [!TIP]
> Individuals with recent rapid weight loss, frequent <u>purging</u>, and severe illness are likely to have laboratory abnormalities, regardless of their body weight. Laboratory findings typically normalize following adequate management. [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[28]](/library/Xm19Vh0)




| <br>Characteristic laboratory abnormalities in eating disorders [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[17]](/library/bm1HVh0)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
|  | Possible findings |
| <u>CBC</u> | <br><br>* <u>Malnutrition</u>: <u>anemia</u>, <u>leukopenia</u>, and/or <u>thrombocytopenia</u><br><br>* <u>Dehydration</u>: may cause <u>hemoconcentration</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Glucose</u> | <br>* <u>Malnutrition</u>: <u>hypoglycemia</u><br><br> |
| <br>Serum <u>electrolytes</u> [[29]](/library/Dn11vh0)[[30]](/library/_bW5wP0)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Malnutrition</u>: ↓ <u>sodium</u>,  ↓ <u>potassium</u>, ↓ <u>chloride</u>, ↑ <u>bicarbonate</u> (<u>metabolic alkalosis</u>), ↓ <u>phosphate</u>, ↓ <u>magnesium</u>, ↓ <u>calcium</u> (mild)<br><br>* <u>Laxative misuse</u>: non <u>anion gap metabolic acidosis</u> (early misuse); <u>metabolic alkalosis</u> (chronic misuse) [[29]](/library/Dn11vh0)<br><br>* <u>Diuretic misuse</u>: ↓ <u>sodium</u>, ↓ <u>potassium</u><br><br>* Recurrent <u>vomiting</u>: <u>hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Renal function tests</u> | <br><br>* <u>Malnutrition</u>: ↑ <u>BUN</u>, ↓ <u>creatinine</u><br><br>* <u>Purging behaviors</u>: ↑ <u>BUN</u>, ↑ <u>creatinine</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Liver function</u> tests | <br>* <u>Malnutrition</u>: ↑ <u>AST</u>, ↑ <u>ALT</u><br><br> |
| Protein | <br><br>* Early <u>malnutrition</u>: ↑ protein, ↑ <u>albumin</u><br><br>* Late <u>malnutrition</u>: ↓ protein, ↓ <u>albumin</u><br><br>* <u>Protein-calorie malnutrition</u> in the past 72 hours: ↓ <u>prealbumin</u> [[17]](/library/bm1HVh0)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Lipid panel</u> | <br>* <u>Malnutrition</u>: ↑ <u>cholesterol</u><br><br> |
| Other | <br><br>* <u>Vomiting</u>: ↑ serum alpha-<u>amylase</u>  [[31]](/library/wn1hvh0)<br><br>* <u>Malnutrition</u>: <u>sick euthyroid syndrome</u><br><br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Hypokalemia</u> can lower the <u>seizure</u> threshold and increase the risk of <u>cardiac arrhythmia</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Normal laboratory study results do not rule out an eating disorder. [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)




#### <u>ECG</u> [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)




* Indications

* Patients with any of the following:

* Abnormal <u>heart rate</u> or blood pressure, <u>orthostasis</u>

* Use of medications that can prolong the <u>QTc</u> interval

* Restrictive eating or severe <u>purging</u>

* <u>Significant weight loss</u>

* <u>Electrolyte</u> abnormalities

* Consider for all patients.  [[17]](/library/bm1HVh0)

* Possible findings [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)

* <u>Malnutrition</u>: <u>bradyarrhythmias</u>, <u>QTc prolongation</u>

* <u>Purging</u>: increased <u>P wave</u> amplitude, <u>wide QRS complex</u>, <u>ST depression</u>, <u>T-wave inversion</u>, <u>SVT</u>, VT





#### <u>Bone densitometry</u> [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)




* Indications

* Patients with any of the following:

* <u>Amenorrhea</u> for ≥ 6 months [[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)[[21]](/library/s_ctpU0)

* <u>Hypogonadism</u> [[5]](/library/b01He20)

* <u>Stress fracture</u> or <u>long bone</u> <u>fracture</u> [[5]](/library/b01He20)

* Male children and <u>adolescents</u> with <u>significant weight loss</u> [[11]](/library/MAbM4w)

* Consider baseline testing for all patients.

* Possible findings: <u>osteopenia</u>, <u>osteoporosis</u> [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)





### Exclusion of organic causes [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)[[5]](/library/b01He20)[[17]](/library/bm1HVh0)




Based on clinical suspicion, evaluate for organic causes of weight changes and eating behaviors, e.g.,




* <u>Thyroid disease</u> or <u>TSH</u> misuse: serum <u>TSH</u>

* <u>IBD</u>: <u>ESR</u>, <u>fecal calprotectin</u>  [[5]](/library/b01He20)[[17]](/library/bm1HVh0)

* <u>Adrenal insufficiency</u>: serum <u>cortisol</u> [[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)

* <u>Diabetes</u>: <u>HbA1c</u>

* <u>PCOS</u>: See “Diagnostics” in <u>PCOS</u>.  [[32]](/library/ao1Q030)

* <u>Celiac disease</u>: <u>celiac panel</u>

* <u>Gastrointestinal infection</u>: <u>stool culture</u>, stool <u>ova</u> and <u>parasites</u> [[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)

* Stimulant misuse: <u>urine toxicology screen</u> [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)

## Disposition

### General principles [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[5]](/library/b01He20)[[13]](/library/y_1dIj0)




* Determination of treatment settings should be based on <u>shared decision-making</u> including the patient, family members, and the care team.  [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)

* Outpatient care is preferred for most patients, if possible.

* Consider the following factors when choosing an initial care setting:

* <u>Red flag features of eating disorders</u>

* Laboratory study abnormalities in eating disorders

* The patient's motivation to change

* The patient's level of control over disordered behaviors

* Psychosocial and <u>cultural factors</u> (e.g., presence of social support)

* Logistical factors (e.g., availability of transportation, insurance barriers)

* Periodically reassess the need for transfer to a higher <u>level of care</u>, e.g., based on :

* Worsening in any of the above factors

* Minimal symptom improvement after ≥ 6 weeks of outpatient care (e.g., < 50% reduction in <u>purging behaviors</u>) [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)





> [!TIP]
> Most eating disorders can be managed in an outpatient setting. [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[33]](/library/sx1tBQ0)




> [!TIP]
> The decision to transfer a patient to another care setting should not be based on weight or <u>BMI</u> alone. [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)




### <u>Red flags</u> supporting hospitalization




The presence of any of the following indicates severe disease and may suggest the need for hospitalization.




| <br>Red flag features of eating disorders [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)[[5]](/library/b01He20)[[13]](/library/y_1dIj0)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | <u>Adolescents</u> and adults < 26 years of age | Adults ≥ 26 years of age |
| Behavior |  | <br><br>* Acute food refusal<br><br>* Frequent, severe compensatory behaviors  [[13]](/library/y_1dIj0)<br><br>* Uncontrolled binge eating<br><br><br> |  |
| <u>BMI</u> |  | <br>* <u>Percent median BMI</u> ≤ 75% for age and sex<br><br> | <br>* < 15 kg/m<sup>2</sup><br><br> |
| Weight loss |  | <br><br>* > 10% weight loss in 6 months<br><br>* > 20% weight loss in 1 year<br><br><br> |  |
| Unstable <u>vital signs</u> | <u>Hypothermia</u> | <br>* Body temperature : < 36Â°C (< 96.8Â°F)<br><br> |  |
| <u>Hypotension</u> | <br>* Blood pressure < 90/45 mm Hg<br><br> | <br>* Blood pressure < 90/60 mm Hg<br><br> |  |
| <u>Bradycardia</u> | <br>* <u>Heart rate</u> < 50 bpm<br><br> |  |  |
| Orthostatic changes | <br>* <u>Orthostatic hypotension</u><br><br> |  |  |
| <br>* Sustained increase in <u>heart rate</u> of > 40 bpm<br><br> | <br>* Sustained increase in <u>heart rate</u> of > 30 bpm<br><br> |  |  |
| Metabolic abnormalities |  | <br><br>* <u>Hypoglycemia</u> (<u>glucose</u> < 60 mg/dL)<br><br>* <u>Electrolyte</u> disturbances (e.g., ↓ serum K, Na, P, Mg)<br><br>* Severe <u>refeeding syndrome</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <u>ECG</u> abnormalities |  | <br>* <u>Arrhythmias</u>, including <u>prolonged QT interval</u> (> 450 ms)<br><br> |  |
| Acute complications |  | <br><br>* Marked <u>dehydration</u><br><br>* Organ dysfunction (e.g., <u>syncope</u>, <u>seizures</u>, <u>pancreatitis</u>, <u>liver</u> failure, <u>heart failure</u>)<br><br><br> |  |
| Other |  | <br><br>* Arrested physical development [[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)[[5]](/library/b01He20)<br><br>* Comorbidities that may inhibit outpatient management<br><br>* Medical: e.g., uncontrolled or <u>type 1 diabetes</u>, <u>substance use disorder</u><br><br>* Psychiatric: e.g., severe <u>depression</u>, <u>suicidality</u><br><br>* No or minimal improvement with outpatient management<br><br><br> |  |





### Treatment settings




#### Inpatient care [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)[[5]](/library/b01He20)




* Candidates include patients:

* With <u>red flag features of eating disorders</u> who require continuous medical monitoring and/or intensive management

* Who require treatment over objection

* Care is provided in either a psychiatric or medical unit, depending on the patient's primary needs.

* Programs with specialized eating disorder care are preferred, if available.





#### Intermediate care [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)[[5]](/library/b01He20)




Candidates include medically stable patients who require intensive guided management by a care team.




* Partial hospitalization

* Patient lives at home but attends a clinic or hospital facility for ≥ 5 hours per day on ≥ 5 days/week. [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)

* Care team monitors most daily meals.

* Residential treatment

* Full-time residence at a facility

* Nursing on-site 24/7 (typically) and a physician <u>on-call</u> 24/7 [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)

* Care team monitors all daily meals.





#### Outpatient care [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)[[3]](/library/i_cJLU0)[[5]](/library/b01He20)




Candidates include medically stable patients with motivation to change and good social support.




* Standard outpatient care

* Intermittent <u>psychotherapy</u> visits (e.g., 1–2 visits/week) [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)

* Meals monitored by caregivers

* Does not interrupt daily living (e.g., school)

* Intensive outpatient care

* Partial day <u>psychotherapy</u> visits (e.g., ≥ 3 visits/week for ≥ 3 hours/visit) [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)

* Care team may monitor meals (e.g., one meal daily). [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)

* Minimal interruption to daily living





> [!TIP]
> Outpatients must have weekly weight monitoring, and patients with <u>purging behavior</u> also require regular monitoring of <u>electrolyte</u> levels. [[2]](/library/Ym1nVh0)
